questions.title: Implementation plan
questions.text: Which statement best describes a **system implementation plan**?

options.content: A document describing how, when and by whom the new system will be installed and put into use
A diagram showing how data flows through the new system
The program code of the new system
A questionnaire used to find the users' requirements

scheme.mark_scheme: A
scheme.explanation: The plan lists every task of the changeover with its order, dates, responsible people, resources and contingency.

questions.title: Why plan the implementation
questions.text: Select **three** reasons why a system implementation plan is important.

options.content: Tasks are done in the correct order and none is forgotten
It removes the need to train staff
Each task has a responsible person and a deadline
It guarantees that the new system has no bugs
Risks such as data loss are planned for with a backup and contingency
It replaces the requirements specification

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: A plan cannot remove bugs or training, but it organises tasks, people, dates and risks.

questions.title: Plan contents
questions.text: Select **two** items that belong in a system implementation plan.

options.content: How data will be transferred from the old system
The source code of every program
The dates on which staff will be trained
The company's marketing strategy

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Elements of the plan
questions.text: Match each element of an implementation plan to what it describes.

right.text: How the old records are transferred and checked
The person in charge of each task
Who is trained, how and when
Start and end dates of each task and the milestones
What to do if the new system fails

scheme.mark_scheme: Schedule – Start and end dates of each task and the milestones; Data conversion – How the old records are transferred and checked; Staff training – Who is trained, how and when; Contingency plan – What to do if the new system fails; Responsibilities – The person in charge of each task. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Which element?
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show which element of the plan the statement belongs to.

prefill: Book records will be imported from the old CSV file
Cashiers attend a 2-hour session on Friday
If the system crashes, staff return to paper receipts
Converted records are checked by double entry

scheme.mark_scheme: Book records will be imported from the old CSV file – Data conversion (1); Go-live is on Monday 24 November – Schedule (1); Cashiers attend a 2-hour session on Friday – Training (1); If the system crashes, staff return to paper receipts – Contingency (1); Converted records are checked by double entry – Data conversion (1)

questions.title: Backup before conversion
questions.text: A full backup of the old data should be made before data conversion begins.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: If the conversion fails, the original data can be restored.

questions.title: Data conversion methods
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the most suitable data conversion method.

prefill: A clinic's patient cards are on paper
The old database can export all records as a CSV file
The old system stores dates and codes in a very different format, for 200 000 records
A small shop's 150 suppliers are written in a notebook

scheme.mark_scheme: A clinic's patient cards are on paper – Manual entry (1); The old database can export all records as a CSV file – Import from files (1); The old system stores dates and codes in a very different format, for 200 000 records – Conversion program (1); A small shop's 150 suppliers are written in a notebook – Manual entry (1)

questions.title: Checking converted data
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

After data is typed in from paper records it is checked by [[1]] entry, where the data is typed twice and the computer compares the two copies, or by a [[2]] check against the original. After an import, the number of [[3]] in the old and new systems is compared.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) double (2) visual / proofreading / proof-reading (3) records / rows
scheme.explanation: Verification checks that data was copied correctly.

questions.title: Training methods
questions.text: Match each training method to an advantage.

right.text: Questions are answered immediately and many staff are trained at once
Staff learn at any time and at their own pace
Training matches the needs of each person

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: When to train
questions.text: When should staff training usually be scheduled in an implementation plan?

options.content: Before the software is installed
Shortly before the new system goes live, after the software is installed
A month after go-live
Only if staff complain

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Staff need the installed software to practise on, and must be able to use it from the first day; training too early is forgotten.

questions.title: Contingency plan
questions.text: What is a **contingency plan** in system implementation?

options.content: The list of hardware to be bought
A plan of what to do if something goes wrong, e.g. restore from backup or return to the old system
The timetable of staff training
The final report on the success of the system

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: A contingency plan reduces risk: if the new system fails or data is lost, the organisation knows what to do.

questions.title: Milestone
questions.text: In an implementation schedule, what is a **milestone**?

options.content: The longest task in the plan
A point in the schedule that marks the end of a stage, e.g. go-live
The person responsible for a task
The budget for hardware

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Milestones have a date but no duration; they are used to check the project is on time.

questions.title: Gantt chart
questions.text: Why is a **Gantt chart** useful in an implementation plan?

options.content: It shows how data flows between processes
It shows when each task starts and ends and which tasks overlap, so progress can be monitored
It shows the structure of the database
It lists the validation rules

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: A Gantt chart is a bar chart of the schedule: time runs left to right, one row per task.

questions.title: Order the tasks
questions.text: Number the tasks **1–5** in the order in which they should be carried out.

prefill: Train staff to use the new system
Review whether the system meets the requirements
Install the software and create user accounts
Go live: start using the new system

scheme.mark_scheme: Install computers and network 1; install software and accounts 2; train staff 3; go live 4; review 5. One mark per correct row.
scheme.explanation: Hardware before software; software before training; training before go-live; the review comes after the system has been used.

questions.title: Dependency
questions.text: In a plan, task 3 is *Install the software and create accounts*, task 4 is *Import the records* and task 5 is *Train staff*. Task 5 "depends on" task 3. Which task must be **finished before** task 5 can start? Give the task number only.

scheme.explanation: A dependency means the task cannot start until the other task has finished: staff need the installed software.

questions.title: Duration of a task
questions.text: A task in an implementation plan starts on **08.11** and ends on **20.11**, counting both days. How many days does it last? Give the number only.

scheme.explanation: 20 − 8 + 1 = 13 days (both the first and the last day are counted).

questions.title: Problems in a plan
questions.text: A café's plan says: *1 Install the tablets (Mon). 2 Go live (Tue). 3 Train the waiters (Wed). 4 Import the menu (Thu).* Nothing else is written. Select the **three** problems with this plan.

options.content: Waiters are trained after the system goes live
The menu is imported after go-live, so orders cannot be taken
There is no responsible person or contingency for any task
The tablets are installed before go-live
The plan has dates

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Training and data conversion must come before go-live, and every task needs a responsible person; a contingency is needed in case the tablets fail.

questions.title: Method and plan
questions.text: If the implementation plan states the implementation method (e.g. parallel running), nothing else needs to be planned.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: The method is only one element: the plan also needs the schedule, installation, data conversion, training, testing, responsibilities and contingency.

questions.title: A new appointment system for a medical centre
questions.text: **Densaulyq Medical Centre** in Karaganda has 12 doctors and 6 receptionists. It is replacing its old appointment software with a new web-based system that also sends SMS reminders to patients. The centre is open six days a week, and patient records must never be lost.

parts.title: Importance
parts.text: Explain **two** reasons why the medical centre should make a system implementation plan.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two reasons, each identified (1) and explained in context (1):
- tasks done in the correct order / none forgotten (1) — e.g. receptionists trained and patient data converted before go-live (1)
- deadlines / milestones so it goes live on time (1) — the centre is open six days a week, so changeover can be planned for Sunday / minimal disruption to patients (1)
- risks reduced (1) — backup and contingency so patient records are never lost (1)
- responsibilities (1) — each person knows their task (1); budget / resources controlled (1)
scheme.model_answer: The plan puts the tasks in the right order, so the patient records are converted and the receptionists trained before the new system is used, and nothing is forgotten. It also plans a backup and contingency, so if the new system fails the centre can restore the patient records and keep booking appointments without losing data.

parts.title: Elements
parts.text: The plan states the implementation method. State **four** other elements that should be included in the plan.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): schedule / timetable / dates; hardware installation; software installation / user accounts; data conversion; staff training (method, timing); acceptance testing; responsibilities; resources / budget; risks / contingency plan; documentation / support; review / evaluation
scheme.model_answer: Schedule of tasks with dates; data conversion; staff training; contingency plan.

parts.title: Responsibilities
parts.text: Explain why the plan names a **responsible person** for each task.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- everyone knows their role / what they must do and by when (1)
- tasks are not forgotten or done twice; the manager knows whom to ask about delays (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each person knows exactly which task they must do and by when, so no task is forgotten or done twice, and the manager knows whom to contact if a task is late.

questions.title: Card payments in a school canteen
questions.text:
A school canteen is introducing a system in which 900 students pay with their student cards. Part of the implementation plan is shown.

| No. | Task | Start | End | Responsible | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Install card readers at 4 tills and Wi-Fi | 02.03 | 04.03 | IT technician | — |
| 2 | Install the payment software; create accounts for 4 cashiers | 05.03 | 06.03 | Supplier | 1 |
| 3 | Import 900 student records and balances | 09.03 | 11.03 | School administrator | 2 |
| 4 | Go live: students pay with cards | 16.03 | 16.03 | Canteen manager | 3 |
| 5 | Train the cashiers | 17.03 | 18.03 | Supplier | 2 |

parts.title: Dependency
parts.text: Identify the task that must be finished before the student records can be imported.

scheme.mark_scheme: Task 2 / install the payment software (1)
scheme.model_answer: Task 2 — installing the payment software and creating the accounts.

parts.title: Durations
parts.text: Complete the table with the duration of each task in days, counting both the start and the end day.

scheme.model_answer: Task 1: 3 days; task 2: 2 days; task 3: 3 days.

parts.title: A problem
parts.text: Identify **one** problem with task 5 and explain its effect.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- cashiers are trained after go-live / task 5 is after task 4 (1)
- on 16.03 cashiers do not know how to use the system, so queues / errors with students' balances (1)
scheme.model_answer: The cashiers are trained on 17.03, after the system goes live on 16.03, so on the first day they do not know how to use it, causing long queues and mistakes with students' balances.

parts.title: Missing task
parts.text: Suggest **one** task that is missing from the plan and explain why it is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any one task (1) with a reason (1):
- back up the old records / balances before import (1) — balances can be restored if the import fails (1)
- verify the imported data (1) — every student's balance must be correct (1)
- acceptance testing / test payments before go-live (1) — faults found before students use it (1)
- tell students how to use cards (1); contingency (cash) if readers fail (1); review (1)
scheme.model_answer: Verify the imported records, e.g. compare the number of students and the total of all balances with the old system, so that every student's balance is correct before they pay.

parts.title: Milestone
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a **milestone** and identify one milestone in this plan.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a point in the schedule that marks the end of a stage / used to check progress (1)
- e.g. go-live on 16.03 / all records imported 11.03 / hardware installed 04.03 (1)
scheme.model_answer: A milestone is an important point in the schedule, with a date but no duration, that marks the end of a stage so progress can be checked — for example the go-live on 16.03.

questions.title: Moving the records of a pharmacy chain
questions.text: **Shipa Pharmacy** has 8 branches. Customer prescriptions for the last 3 years are stored in an old database, but the **supplier list** is kept on paper cards. A new stock and prescription system will replace both.

parts.title: Conversion methods
parts.text: Describe **two** methods the pharmacy could use to convert its data. Refer to its records in your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two methods, each described (1) and linked to the pharmacy's data (1):
- import / export (1) — prescriptions exported from the old database as files (e.g. CSV) and imported into the new one (1)
- manual entry (1) — supplier cards typed in by staff (1)
- conversion program (1) — written to change the old prescription format into the new format (1)
scheme.model_answer: The prescriptions can be exported from the old database as a CSV file and imported into the new system automatically. The paper supplier cards must be typed in manually by staff.

parts.title: Verification
parts.text: Explain why the converted data must be verified, and describe **one** method of verification.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- errors / data loss can happen when typing or importing (1)
- wrong prescriptions / stock could harm customers or cause losses (1)
- method described: double entry — typed twice and compared / visual check against the cards / compare record counts or totals between old and new systems (1)
scheme.model_answer: Records can be mistyped or lost during conversion, and a wrong prescription could harm a customer. After the import the number of prescription records in the old and new systems is compared, and supplier cards are checked visually against the screen.

parts.title: Contingency
parts.text: Suggest **one** risk during the changeover and a contingency action for it. Explain why the action reduces the risk.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- risk, e.g. import fails / data lost / new system crashes / branch loses connection (1)
- action, e.g. full backup before conversion and restore / keep old system running / paper procedure (1)
- explanation linked: pharmacy can still serve customers / no prescriptions lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: The import may corrupt some prescriptions. A full backup of the old database is made before conversion, so if this happens the data can be restored and the import repeated, and no customer's prescription history is lost.

questions.title: A membership system for a sports centre
questions.text: **Olimp Sports Centre** has 25 staff who work in shifts from 07:00 to 23:00, and 3 000 members whose details are on paper forms. It is introducing a new membership system with card entry at the door. The manager wants the changeover to finish within **six weeks** and must keep the centre open.

parts.title: Training methods
parts.text: Compare **two** methods of training the staff. Refer to the sports centre in your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two methods compared, up to 4 marks, with points linked to shifts:
- classroom / group session: questions answered immediately (1) but staff on different shifts cannot all attend / centre short of staff (1)
- online videos / tutorials: any time, suits shift work, cheap to repeat (1) but no immediate help (1)
- train the trainer: key staff on each shift train colleagues (1); one-to-one: suits needs but slow for 25 staff (1)
Max 2 if not compared / not in context.
scheme.model_answer: A group session with a trainer lets staff ask questions straight away, but because staff work shifts from 07:00 to 23:00 they cannot all attend at once without closing the centre. Online video tutorials can be watched at any time between shifts, so the centre stays open, but staff cannot ask questions immediately.

parts.title: Make a plan
parts.text: Make a system implementation plan for the sports centre. Include the tasks in a suitable order, with an approximate timing and the person responsible, the training of staff, the conversion of the members' data and a contingency.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 6 marks:
- hardware (card readers / PCs) installed first, before software (1)
- software installed, accounts created (1)
- member data converted by manual entry from paper forms and verified (double entry / visual check), with a backup / copies of forms kept (1)
- staff trained before go-live, suited to shifts (1)
- timings within six weeks in a sensible order, each task with a responsible person (1)
- contingency (e.g. paper sign-in / manual check if card readers fail) or acceptance testing / review after go-live (1)
scheme.model_answer: Week 1: IT technician installs card readers at the door and PCs at reception. Week 2: supplier installs the software and creates staff accounts. Weeks 2–4: two receptionists type in the 3 000 paper forms; each record is checked visually against its form and the forms are kept as a backup. Week 4: staff watch the online tutorials and each shift leader runs a short hands-on session. Week 5: acceptance testing with test members; go-live on Monday of week 5. Contingency: if a card reader fails, staff check members in by name on the paper list. Week 6: the manager reviews the system with staff.

summary: Why a system implementation plan is important, what it contains (method, schedule, hardware and software installation, data conversion, staff training, testing, responsibilities, risks and support), and how to make an implementation plan with a task table, dependencies, milestones and a Gantt chart.

blocks.content: The stage of the system life cycle in which the new system is **installed, the data is transferred, users are trained and the organisation changes over** from the old system to the new one.

A document that describes **how, when and by whom** a new system will be **installed and put into use**, replacing the old system. It lists **every task**, its **order**, **dates**, the **people responsible**, the **resources** needed and what to do **if something goes wrong**.

Implementing a new system involves many people (developers, managers, staff, suppliers) and many tasks that depend on each other: the hardware must be installed before the software, the data must be converted before the system goes live, staff must be trained before they use it. Without a plan, tasks are forgotten, done in the wrong order or late.

blocks.text: Why the plan matters: each reason explained

blocks.content: **Tasks are not forgotten.** Implementation is a long list of small jobs: buying cables, creating user accounts, copying thousands of records, printing user guides, booking a room for training. Each one is easy, but if a single job is forgotten the system cannot start. Writing every task in a plan turns a vague goal ("start the new system in November") into a checklist that can be ticked off.

**Tasks happen in the right order.** Many tasks **depend** on others. Software cannot be installed on computers that have not arrived; data cannot be imported into a database that does not exist; staff cannot practise on a system that is not installed. The plan shows these dependencies, so nobody waits for a task that has not started and nobody starts a task too early.

**The system goes live on time.** A plan gives every task a start date, an end date and a duration, and marks **milestones** such as "all data converted" or "go-live". Managers compare the real progress with the plan every week. If a task is late they see it **early**, while there is still time to add staff or move other tasks, instead of discovering on the go-live day that nothing is ready.

**Everyone knows their role.** Implementation involves the developer, the IT technician, the supplier, managers and ordinary staff. When each task has a **responsible person**, work is not done twice and no task is left with "I thought you were doing that".

**Cost and resources are controlled.** The plan lists the equipment, the trainers and the staff time each task needs. Staff who enter data or attend training are not doing their normal work, so the organisation must plan cover for them. Knowing the resources in advance keeps the project inside its **budget**.

**Risk and disruption are reduced.** The changeover is the most dangerous moment in the life of a system: real data and real customers meet the new software for the first time. The plan makes sure a **backup** exists, that the data is **verified**, that the system is **tested** before go-live, and that there is a **contingency plan** if it fails. It also schedules disruptive work at quiet times — a shop installs new tills on a Sunday night, a school changes its system during the holidays — so that normal work continues.
**Success can be checked.** Because the plan states what should be achieved and by when, a **review** after go-live can compare the result with the plan and with the original requirements.

blocks.title: Why a clinic needs a plan
blocks.content: A clinic in Karaganda replaces its paper appointment book with an online booking system. Without a plan, the receptionists are trained after the system goes live, the old appointments for next month are not entered, and on Monday morning patients arrive for appointments the new system does not know about. With a plan, the existing appointments are **backed up and entered** in the week before go-live and **checked** against the paper book, the receptionists are **trained on Thursday and Friday**, the system goes live on **Monday at 08:00**, and the paper book is kept for two weeks as a **contingency**. The same work is done, but in the right order and with a safety net.

blocks.caption: Where the implementation plan fits in the system life cycle

items.title: Why the plan is important
items.content:
- Makes sure **no task is forgotten** (data conversion, training, backups).
- Puts tasks in the **correct order** and shows **dependencies**.
- Sets **deadlines** and **milestones** so the system goes live **on time**.
- Gives each task a **responsible person** — everyone knows their role.
- Controls the **budget** and **resources** (equipment, staff time, trainers).
- **Reduces risk**: plans a **backup** and what to do if the new system fails (contingency).
- **Minimises disruption** to the organisation's normal work (e.g. installing at weekends).
- Allows managers to **monitor progress** and check the implementation was successful.

items.title: What can go wrong without a plan
items.content:
- Staff are **not trained** when the system starts, so mistakes are made.
- **Data is lost** or entered incorrectly during conversion.
- Hardware arrives **late**, so the go-live date is missed.
- No **backup** of the old system — the business stops if the new one fails.
- Costs run **over budget**; two teams do the same job while another is forgotten.

blocks.title: Implementation with and without a plan
rows: Software installed before the network is ready; training after go-live
Go-live date missed; staff do not know when to prepare
Old records lost or copied with errors
The business stops if the new system fails
**Contingency plan**: fall back to the old system or the backup
Nobody checks whether the system works as required
**Review** against the requirements on a set date

blocks.content: The **method** (direct, parallel, pilot, phased) is only **one element** of the plan. A plan that says only "we will use parallel running" is not a plan: it also needs the schedule, installation, data conversion, training, testing, responsibilities and contingency.

blocks.title: Elements of a system implementation plan
rows: Direct, parallel, pilot or phased — and why it was chosen
Parallel running for 4 weeks — loans must not be lost
The tasks, their **start and end dates**, their order and **milestones** (often a Gantt chart)
What equipment is bought and installed, where, and when
Installing and configuring the application, OS, database; **user accounts and access rights**
How data is **transferred** from the old system and how it is **checked**
2 400 book records typed in, double entry
**Who** is trained, the **method**, the **timing**, who runs it
Final **acceptance testing** with the client; checking converted data
Test loans and returns with the librarian
The person or team responsible for each task
What could go wrong and what to do
Restore from backup; continue on paper
User guide, technical documentation, help desk after go-live
Quick guide at the desk; developer on call
How and when the success of the implementation will be checked

blocks.content: The **method** decides the shape of the whole plan. With **direct changeover** everything — data conversion, training, testing — must be finished before one fixed date, so the schedule is tight and the contingency plan is critical. With **parallel running** the plan must include the period when staff work in **both** systems, the extra staff time this needs and the date when results are compared and the old system is switched off. With **pilot** or **phased** implementation the plan repeats installation and training for each department or each part of the system.

The **schedule** turns the list of tasks into dates. It shows the start and end of every task, the tasks that can run at the same time and the milestones. **Hardware installation** comes early because almost everything else depends on it; it includes delivery, cabling, connecting the devices and checking that they work. **Software installation** includes installing the application and the database, configuring settings, and creating **user accounts with access rights**, so that each member of staff sees only what they need — a receptionist can book appointments, but only a doctor can read medical notes.

**Testing before go-live** is the last check that the system is ready. The client tries real tasks with the converted data — this is **acceptance testing** — and confirms the system meets the requirements. Only after the client accepts it does the system go live. **Documentation and support** continue after go-live: users need a guide to look things up, technicians need technical documentation, and someone must answer questions in the first busy weeks. Finally the **review** compares the new system with the requirements: is it faster, are there fewer errors, are users satisfied?

Testing of the finished system **by the client and the users**, with real or realistic data, to confirm that it **meets the requirements** before it goes live. If the client accepts the system, the go-live milestone can be reached.

Transferring the existing data from the **old system** (paper records or old files) into the **new system**, in the **format** the new system needs, and **checking** that it was transferred **completely and correctly**.

blocks.caption: Data conversion: back up, transfer, check, then go live

blocks.title: Data conversion methods
rows: **Manual entry** — typing data from paper records
No special software needed; data can be tidied while typing
Slow, needs staff time; typing errors
**Import / export** — data copied from old files into the new database (CSV, SQL scripts)
Fast for thousands of records; fewer typing errors
Formats may not match; faulty records copied too
Compare **record counts and totals**; sample checks
**Conversion program** written to change the format
Old and new formats are very different
Must be written and tested — extra cost
Test the program on a **copy** first

blocks.content: Always make a **full backup of the old data** before conversion begins, so nothing is lost if the conversion fails. Then **verify** the converted data — compare the number of records, totals (e.g. the sum of all balances) and a sample of records with the originals.

A new system only brings benefits if people **use it correctly**. Staff who do not know how to do their everyday tasks make errors, work slowly and lose confidence in the system; some go back to their old ways of working. Training is therefore a separate element of the plan, with its own **method, timing, trainer and resources**.

The **method** is chosen to fit the staff and the organisation. A large group with the same tasks — thirty teachers learning an electronic register — can be trained together in a classroom session. A manager who needs only reports can be shown one-to-one. Staff who work shifts, such as nurses, benefit from online videos they can watch at any time. Many organisations combine methods: a short group session, a quick guide on every desk and a practice mode for trying things without risk.

The **timing** matters as much as the method. Training given months before go-live is forgotten; training given after go-live means staff learn on real customers. The plan therefore puts training **after the software is installed** (there must be something to practise on) and **just before go-live**, with refresher help in the first weeks. Training is usually arranged in groups or shifts so that the organisation keeps working while some staff are away.

blocks.title: Staff training methods
rows: Questions answered immediately; many staff at once
Staff away from work; one pace for all
Any time, at the learner's own pace; cheap to repeat
No immediate help; staff may skip it
Some people do not read them
**"Train the trainer"** — key users train colleagues
Quality depends on the key users
Hands-on with realistic data, no risk

items.title: Who is trained
items.content:
- **Users** — how to do their everyday tasks.
- **Managers** — reports and settings.
- **Technical staff** — backups, accounts, fixing faults.

items.title: When
items.content:
- **Before go-live**, close to it, so staff remember.
- Refresher sessions and help **after** go-live.
- Outside busy hours / in shifts so work continues.

blocks.content: A task that **cannot start until another task has finished** — e.g. staff training depends on the software being installed. Dependencies decide the **order** of the tasks.

An important **point in the schedule** that marks the **end of a stage**, with a date but no duration — e.g. "hardware installed", "go-live", "old system switched off". Managers use milestones to check that the project is **on time**.
A plan of **what to do if something goes wrong** during implementation — e.g. restore the data from the backup, go back to the old system, use a temporary manual procedure.

The hardest part of making a plan is deciding the **order** of the tasks. Start with the end: the **go-live** date. Ask what must be finished before go-live — the data converted and checked, the staff trained, the system tested. Then ask what each of those needs before it can start: training needs the software installed; the software needs the hardware; data conversion needs the database and a backup of the old data. Working backwards like this produces a chain of **dependencies**.

Next, estimate the **duration** of each task. Some durations can be calculated: if one assistant can type 100 book records an hour and there are 2 400 books, data entry takes 24 hours of work — with two assistants working 4 hours a day, about 3 days. Others are estimated from experience or from the supplier (delivery takes 5 working days). It is sensible to add a little **spare time** to risky tasks.

Tasks that do not depend on each other can be done **at the same time**, which shortens the project. For example, the backup of old records and the installation of the hardware can happen together, and staff training can start while the last records are typed in. The longest chain of dependent tasks from start to go-live decides the **earliest possible go-live date**: if any task in that chain is late, the go-live is late. Managers watch these tasks most closely.

Once the order and durations are known, each task gets a **start date**, an **end date** and a **responsible person**, and the milestones are added. The plan is then drawn as a **table** (for the details) and a **Gantt chart** (for the timeline). The plan is not fixed for ever: when something is late, the plan is updated and everyone is told the new dates.

The **longest chain of dependent tasks** from the start of the project to its end. It gives the shortest possible time to finish; a delay to any task on the critical path delays the whole implementation.

blocks.title: How to write the plan
items: Choose the **implementation method** and justify it for the organisation.
List **all tasks**: backup, hardware, software and accounts, data conversion, training, testing, go-live, support, review.
Put the tasks in **order** and note which depend on others.
Estimate the **duration** of each task and set **dates** and **milestones**.
Assign a **responsible person** to each task.
Show the plan as a **table** and a **Gantt chart**.

blocks.title: Reading the plan
blocks.content:
- Task 4 lasts **13 days** (08.11 – 20.11, counting both days).
- Tasks 4 and 5 **overlap** (18.11 – 20.11): staff are trained while the last records are typed in.
- Task 7 depends on tasks 4 **and** 5 — testing cannot start until the data is entered and the staff are trained.
- If the scanners (task 2) arrive late, tasks 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 all move later — the go-live **milestone** is missed.

blocks.title: Contingency plan
rows: The new system crashes during parallel running
Continue with the paper system; developer fixes the fault
Data entry takes longer than planned
Two more assistants; parallel running starts later
Use keyboard entry of barcodes temporarily
Restore from the backup made in task 1
Key member of staff ill on training day
Second session / video recording of the training

blocks.content:
- Training staff **after** the go-live date.
- Data conversion **before** the software is installed, or **no backup** before conversion.
- Tasks with **no dates** or **no responsible person**.
- No **acceptance testing** before go-live.
- No **contingency** — "nothing will go wrong".
- Stopping the old system **before** the new one has been checked.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: The system implementation plan specifies the method of implementing the new system. State two more elements that are described in this plan. [2]**
Determine the **training method** for personnel (1); determine the **timing of staff training** / plan for **installation of the application** / **data conversion** / **schedule** / **responsible persons** (1).

**Q: Explain the importance of making a system implementation plan. [2]**
It makes sure all tasks — installation, data conversion, training — are done in the **correct order and on time** (1), so the changeover causes **little disruption** and **risks** such as data loss are reduced (1).

**Q: Explain why data should be verified after conversion. [2]**
Errors can be made when **copying or typing** the data into the new system (1); verification (double entry / comparing record counts with the original) ensures the new system starts with **accurate data** (1).

**Q: A clinic's plan schedules staff training on the day after go-live. Explain why this is a problem and suggest a change. [3]**
Staff would use the system **without knowing how** (1), so they make mistakes with appointments / patients wait (1). Move training to the days **just before** go-live / after the software is installed (1).

**Q: Explain what is meant by a milestone and give an example. [2]**
A point in the schedule marking the **end of a stage**, used to check progress (1), e.g. "go-live on 24.11" / "all data converted" (1).

**Q: Describe a contingency plan for a shop changing over to a new sales system. [2]**
If the new system fails, the shop **returns to the old tills / manual receipts** (1) and restores data **from the backup** made before the changeover (1).

- Listing only the **method** — the plan also covers schedule, installation, data conversion, training, testing and contingency.
- Training staff **after** the system goes live.
- Forgetting to **back up** the old data before conversion.
- A plan without **dates** or **responsible people**.
- Answers about "the system" in general — link each point to the **scenario** (clinic, shop, school).

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define a system implementation plan and give four reasons why it is important.
List ten elements of an implementation plan.
Describe three methods of data conversion and how the converted data is checked.
Compare four methods of staff training; when should training happen?
Define dependency, milestone, contingency plan and Gantt chart.
Write an implementation plan (tasks, dates, responsible person, dependencies) and draw a Gantt chart for a new attendance system in a school.
